Indeed, it must have been an honest strive to uphold standards befitting a college which led President Halsell and his faculty to make such a clear distinction between degrees and diplomas—that degrees were not conferred casually or promiscuously; in fact, few remaining ex-students have been found who received their degrees. The A.B. degrees of W. J. Hunt, shown in the reduced photograph in this chapter, conferred in 1887, was labeled No. 3. The fact that three students who earned their degrees from the institution—among them Mr. Warren and Mr. Roy Dobbins—were later on its faculty is indicative of the respect in which the degree was regarded.

Pedagogical Methods.

The Predominant Recitation Method.—The second of the General Rules of the College catalog stated that:

    2. It is made obligatory on each pupil to be able to recite at least satisfactorily in all his studies, and any one failing to do so will be dropped to a lower grade.⁴²

    This rule was indicative of the predominant method of teaching two generations ago—the recitation method—which still maintained a firm hold, for "reciting the lesson" it was, in the Primary and Preparatory departments of that, of course, then, Savoy College would appear to have been fallen in with the individual Collegiate departments.

    The recitation room was also a study hall, for each faculty member presided over his or her (she was individually identified by his name rather than number or division) and each student was individually assigned to a teacher, who was expected to remain there all during the school hours doing reciting primarily to the recitation benches of the various professors according to schedule, and to other parts of the buildings in many cases, from their seats in the room. Pupils in the lower-class and from their seats there recited all their lessons—all had been in charge of class room.

⁴²Catalogue of Savoy Literary College, op. cit., p. 12.
